title: Translating Language Constructs to Intermediate Representation

blocks.text: Imagine transforming high-level language constructs like loops and conditionals into a form that a machine can easily understand and optimize. This is the power of Intermediate Representation (IR).

blocks.markdown: In compiler design, Intermediate Representation (IR) serves as a bridge between high-level source code and machine code. It allows for easier analysis and optimization. In this lesson, we'll explore how to translate common language constructs such as conditionals, loops, arrays, and procedure calls into IR, specifically using three-address code (TAC) with labels.

blocks.title: Three-Address Code (TAC)
blocks.text: Three-address code is a type of intermediate representation used in compilers, where each instruction contains at most three addresses or operands.

blocks.latex:
t1 = x > y 
\text{if } t1 \text{ goto } L1 
  z = y 
goto L2 
L1: z = x 
L2:
blocks.caption: Three-address code for an if-else construct.

blocks.markdown: Next, we will look at generating address computation for an array access. Consider the array access `a[i]` in a high-level language. To translate this into IR, we need to compute the address of the element.

blocks.title: Array Address Computation
blocks.text: The address of an element `a[i]` can be computed using the formula: `base_address + i * element_size`, where `base_address` is the starting address of the array and `element_size` is the size of each element.

blocks.markdown: Finally, we will describe the IR produced for a procedure call and return. Consider a function call `foo(a, b)` and its return statement `return x`.

blocks.title: Procedure Call and Return
blocks.text: For a procedure call, arguments are typically evaluated and stored in temporary variables, followed by a call instruction. The return value is handled by storing it in a designated location.

blocks.latex:
t1 = a 
t2 = b 
call foo, t1, t2 
return x
blocks.caption: Three-address code for a procedure call and return.

points: Three-address code simplifies translation of high-level constructs into IR.
Conditionals and loops are translated using labels and temporary variables.
Array accesses require address computation using base address and element size.
Procedure calls involve argument evaluation and designated return handling.
